fields.foundation: The Ming Empire was founded in 1368 by Zhu Yuanzhang, a former peasant and Buddhist novice who rose to prominence during the collapse of the Yuan dynasty. The Mongol-led Yuan had been weakened by internal strife, fiscal mismanagement, devastating Yellow River floods and widespread uprisings, and regional warlords and rebel leaders seized power. Zhu came out of the Red Turban Rebellion (c. 1351–1368). He took Nanjing in 1356 and unified southern China by defeating his rivals, above all Chen Youliang at the great naval battle of Lake Poyang in 1363 and Zhang Shicheng in 1367. In January 1368 he proclaimed the Ming dynasty at Nanjing, reigning as the Hongwu Emperor, and later that year his armies captured the Yuan capital, Dadu (Khanbaliq, modern Beijing), and drove the Mongol court back to the steppe. He centralised government, renewed Confucian ideology and consolidated his territory. The early dynasty relied on disciplined military organisation and administrative restructuring, and claimed legitimacy by reasserting Han Chinese traditions. Control of the Yangtze and Yellow River basins, together with the support of leading regional elites, enabled the Ming to stabilise China and begin a period of growth.
fields.socioeconomy: The Ming social and economic order kept much from earlier dynasties and added new methods of administration. Society was ranked, with the emperor at the top, followed by scholar-officials recruited through the civil service examinations, the local gentry, peasants and artisans; merchants held an ambiguous status despite their wealth. The economy rested on agriculture: rice, wheat and millet, supplemented by cotton, sericulture and, from the late 16th century, New World crops such as maize and sweet potatoes. The state compiled land surveys (the fish-scale registers) and population registers (the yellow registers) and organised households under the lijia system to assess taxes and labour service. Domestic markets thrived, and in the early 15th century the Yongle Emperor sponsored Zheng He's voyages to Southeast Asia, India and East Africa. Revenue came from taxes in kind and later in silver, consolidated in the Single Whip reforms of the 16th century, and from the salt monopoly. Silver imported from Japan and, via Manila, from Spanish America monetised the economy and fed population growth, urbanisation and commercial expansion, especially in the Yangtze delta.
fields.military: The Ming military grew into a large, highly organised force of infantry, artillery and cavalry. The early Ming adopted some Mongol practices but organised its forces into hereditary military households under the Weisuo system of garrisons, which was meant to make soldier-farmers self-supporting. Garrison towns along the northern frontier, and the long brick-faced walls built mainly in the 16th century and now known as the Great Wall, show a growing emphasis on defence, especially after the Zhengtong Emperor was captured by the Oirat Mongols at Tumu in 1449. Infantry used crossbows, pikes and gunpowder weapons including cannon and firearms such as hand cannons, while cavalry provided mobility and rapid response. Campaigns included the Yongle Emperor's five expeditions into Mongolia, the occupation of Vietnam (1407–1427), the suppression of coastal pirates (wokou) by commanders such as Qi Jiguang, and the intervention in Korea against the Japanese invasions of 1592–1598. Zheng He's fleets also carried Ming naval power across the Indian Ocean. Military strength kept order at home and gave the Ming influence abroad, and allowed it to govern a large and diverse empire.
fields.governance: Government in the Ming Empire was highly centralised under the emperor, who was supported by an extensive bureaucracy trained in Confucian principles. After abolishing the office of chancellor in 1380, the Hongwu Emperor ruled directly through the Six Ministries. Under his successors a Grand Secretariat developed to assist the throne, and palace eunuchs gained increasing influence. Officials selected through the civil service examinations administered provinces, prefectures and counties, which gave government a meritocratic character. The state maintained detailed population and tax registers, and the law was codified in the Great Ming Code (Da Ming Lü). Central ministries coordinated military, fiscal and ritual affairs, while a Censorate monitored the conduct of officials. The emperor retained supreme authority and could override bureaucratic decisions, yet the administrative structure kept law and the allocation of resources fairly uniform. Justice combined statutory law with Confucian norms. With central authority and a professional bureaucracy, the Ming state could mobilise resources efficiently for defence and infrastructure across a territory of some 6 million square kilometres at its height.
fields.impact: The Ming Empire had great influence in East Asia and beyond during the early modern period. At home, the restoration of Han Chinese rule reinforced Confucian social order and cultural continuity. The circulation of silver, silk and porcelain tied China to East Asian, Indian Ocean and, from the 16th century, global trade networks, and Ming blue-and-white porcelain was prized from Persia to Europe. Zheng He's expeditions (1405–1433) extended China's diplomatic and commercial reach to Southeast Asia, South Asia, Arabia and East Africa, establishing tributary relations and displaying imperial prestige. Ming relations with Korea, Vietnam, Japan and Central Asian states affected regional alliances, trade and cultural exchange. The Yongle Emperor moved the capital to Beijing, where the Forbidden City was completed in 1420, restored the Grand Canal to supply it, and sponsored the very large Yongle Encyclopedia. The Ming legacy persisted in Chinese government, in Neo-Confucian thought such as that of Wang Yangming, in vernacular novels and the arts, and in the institutions of successor dynasties and neighbouring states.
fields.decline: The Ming Empire declined through internal mismanagement, fiscal strain and external pressure. By the late 16th century, the long withdrawal of the Wanli Emperor from government, eunuch influence and factional struggles such as those between the Donglin faction and its opponents had weakened the bureaucracy, while the costs of border defence and of the Korean war strained state finances. Cold weather associated with the Little Ice Age brought repeated droughts, floods and famines, and a fall in silver imports in the 1630s deepened the crisis. Peasant uprisings followed, among them the Li Zicheng rebellion and that of Zhang Xianzhong. Meanwhile the Manchus, united under Nurhaci and Hong Taiji, pressed on the north-east frontier. In April 1644 Li Zicheng's rebels captured Beijing and the Chongzhen Emperor took his own life; the Ming general Wu Sangui then allied with the Manchus, who defeated Li at Shanhai Pass and occupied Beijing, establishing the Qing dynasty there. Ming loyalists in the south formed the Southern Ming regimes, which survived in fragmented form until 1662. Ming administration, culture and technology nevertheless continued to influence China and East Asia long after the dynasty's fall.
fields.summary: The Ming Empire restored Han Chinese rule after the Mongol Yuan. Its Confucian bureaucracy, northern defences and the voyages of Zheng He influenced East Asia long after the dynasty fell to rebellion and the Manchu capture of Beijing in 1644.
fields.teaser: The Ming Dynasty built the Forbidden City and the final Great Wall, restored Chinese sovereignty after Mongol rule, and launched Zheng He's naval expeditions.
fields.t0: The Ming dynasty restored Han Chinese rule in 1368 after driving the Mongol Yuan court back to the steppe.
fields.t1: Its examination-based bureaucracy, Zheng He's voyages and global silver trade made it a centre of the early modern world.
fields.t2: Fiscal crisis, famine and rebellion let Li Zicheng take Beijing in 1644, opening the way for the Manchu Qing.
fields.dyk: The Ming Great Wall seen by visitors today is largely a 16th-century brick-faced work, built after the Zhengtong Emperor was captured by the Oirats at Tumu in 1449.
